The administration of doses that induce fetal toxicity during pregnancy has been associated with the observation of ventricular septal defects at levels linked to severe maternal toxicity. 2. Both nevirapine and delavirdine are classified as FDA Pregnancy Category C drugs. 3. Phase I studies of several protease inhibitors (e.g., indinavir, ritonavir, nelfinavir, and saquinavir) in combination with ZDV and 3TC in pregnant women and their infants are ongoing in the United States. However, no data are currently available regarding the dosage, safety, or tolerance of these protease inhibitors in pregnant women or neonates. 4. Indinavir demonstrates substantial placental passage in mice, but minimal placental passage has been observed in rabbits, according to unpublished data from Merck Research Laboratories. 5. Ritonavir has shown some placental passage in rats, based on unpublished data from Abbott Laboratories. 6. The placental transfer of saquinavir in rats and rabbits is minimal, as per unpublished data from Hoffman-La Roche, Inc. 7. No data are available on the placental passage of nelfinavir in rodents, and the transplacental passage of any protease inhibitors in humans remains unknown. 8. Administration of indinavir to pregnant rodents has not resulted in teratogenicity. However, treatment-related increases in the incidence of supernumerary and cervical ribs have been observed in the offspring of pregnant rodents receiving indinavir at doses comparable to those administered to humans. 9. In pregnant rats receiving high doses of ritonavir associated with maternal toxicity, developmental toxicity was observed in their offspring, including decreased fetal weight, delayed skeletal ossification, wavy ribs, enlarged fontanelles, and cryptorchidism. In rabbits, only decreased fetal weight and viability were observed when ritonavir was administered at maternally toxic doses. 10. Studies in rodents have not demonstrated embryotoxicity or teratogenicity associated with saquinavir or nelfinavir. 11. Indinavir is associated with infrequent side effects in adults, such as hyperbilirubinemia and renal stones, which could pose risks to newborns if transplacental passage occurs and the drug is administered near the time of delivery. 12. Due to the immature hepatic metabolic enzymes in neonates, indinavir would likely have a prolonged half-life, potentially exacerbating the physiological hyperbilirubinemia observed in neonates. 13. 14. These concerns are theoretical, as such side effects have not been reported. 15. Because the half-life of indinavir in adults is short, these concerns may only be relevant if the drug is administered near the time of delivery. 16. Saquinavir, ritonavir, and nelfinavir are classified as FDA Pregnancy Category B drugs, while indinavir is classified as Category C. 17. The FDA has issued a public health advisory regarding the association of diabetes mellitus, hyperglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, and exacerbation of pre-existing diabetes mellitus with the administration of protease inhibitor antiretroviral drugs in HIV-infected individuals. 18. Pregnancy itself is a risk factor for hyperglycemia, and it is unknown whether the use of protease inhibitors will exacerbate the risk of pregnancy-associated hyperglycemia. 19. Healthcare providers caring for HIV-infected pregnant women receiving protease inhibitor therapy should be aware of the potential for hyperglycemia and closely monitor glucose levels in these patients. 20. 21. In 1996, final results were reported for all 419 infants enrolled in PACTG 076. 22. The results confirmed those initially reported in 1994, with a Kaplan-Meier estimated HIV transmission rate of 22.6% for infants receiving placebo compared to 7.6% for those receiving ZDV, representing a 66% reduction in transmission risk. 23. The mechanism by which ZDV reduces transmission in PACTG 076 has not been fully defined. 24. The effect of ZDV on maternal HIV-1 RNA does not fully account for its observed efficacy in reducing transmission. 25. 26. If so, transplacental passage of antiretroviral drugs would be crucial for preventing transmission. 27. In placental perfusion studies, ZDV has been metabolized into the active triphosphate form within the placenta, which could provide additional protection against in utero transmission. 28. This phenomenon may be unique to ZDV, as metabolism to the active triphosphate form within the placenta has not been observed in other nucleoside analogues evaluated, such as ddI and ddC. 29. The presence of ZDV-resistant virus was not necessarily associated with failure to prevent transmission. 30. In a preliminary evaluation of genotypic resistance in pregnant women in PACTG 076, ZDV-resistant virus was present at delivery in only one of seven women who transmitted the virus to their newborns, had received ZDV, and had evaluable samples. This woman had ZDV-resistant virus at the start of the study despite no prior ZDV therapy. 31. Additionally, the one woman in this evaluation whose virus developed genotypic resistance to ZDV during the study period did not transmit HIV-1 to her infant. 32. 33. Data from the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry also demonstrated no increased risk of congenital abnormalities among infants born to women receiving ZDV antenatally compared to the general population. 34. Data for uninfected infants from PACTG 076 followed from birth to a median age of 3.9 years indicated no differences in growth, neurodevelopment, or immunologic status among infants born to mothers who received ZDV compared to those born to mothers who received placebo. 35. 36. 37. 38. The effect of temporary ZDV administration during pregnancy to reduce perinatal transmission on the induction of viral resistance to ZDV and long-term maternal health requires further evaluation. 39. Preliminary data from an interim analysis of PACTG protocol 288 (a study following women enrolled in PACTG 076 through 3 years postpartum) indicate no substantial differences at 18 months postpartum in CD4+ T-lymphocyte count or clinical status in women who received ZDV compared to those who received placebo. 40. Limited data regarding the development of genotypic ZDV-resistance mutations (e.g., codons 70 and/or 215) are available from a subset of women in PACTG 076 who received ZDV.
